qs.q: What is the specific enzymatic effect of insulin in the liver concerning glycogen metabolism?
o: It inhibits glycogen phosphorylase and activates glycogen synthase
It activates both glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase
It inhibits both glycogen phosphorylase and glycogen synthase
It activates glycogen phosphorylase and inhibits glycogen synthase
qs.e: Insulin promotes glycogen storage in the liver by inhibiting glycogen phosphorylase (which breaks down glycogen) and activating glycogen synthase (which promotes glycogen formation). This ensures net glycogen accumulation.

qs.q: Which of the following is classified as a lysosomal storage disorder that does NOT involve abnormal glycogen metabolism?
qs.e: Tay Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disorder classified as a sphingolipidosis and does not involve glycogen metabolism. Pompe and Von Gierke diseases are directly related to glycogen storage abnormalities.

faq.a: Glucose‑6‑phosphatase deficiency forces glucose‑6‑phosphate into glycolysis, producing excess lactate.
faq.q: Why does a patient with GSD I have high lactate?

faq.a: After a brief period of fatigue, patients with GSD V switch to oxidative metabolism using blood glucose, improving exercise tolerance.
Yes; parasite consumption of glucose and hepatic dysfunction can lower blood glucose, especially with quinine therapy.

exam: A 6‑month‑old presents with seizures after overnight fast — explain the metabolic pathway involved and the most likely diagnosis — GSD I; deficiency of glucose‑6‑phosphatase causing impaired glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

A 22‑year‑old reports muscle pain after sprinting but feels better after 10 minutes of walking — what condition does this suggest and why? — GSD V; lack of muscle phosphorylase prevents rapid glycogen breakdown, second‑wind occurs via blood glucose.

In a patient with severe malaria, bedside glucose is 55 mg/dL. What immediate step is required and why? — Give rapid oral or IV glucose to prevent neuroglycopenia; malaria can precipitate hypoglycaemia.
How does insulin affect glycogen synthase and glycogen phosphorylase? — Insulin activates phosphatase → dephosphorylates synthase (on) and phosphorylase (off).

A child with hepatomegaly has normal fasting glucose but elevated lactate; which test would you order if available and what would you expect? — Measure serum uric acid; expect elevation in GSD I due to impaired gluconeogenesis.
Why is high‑intensity exercise contraindicated in McArdle disease? — It relies on rapid glycogen breakdown, which is absent, leading to early fatigue and possible rhabdomyolysis.
What alternative management is possible when a lactate assay is unavailable? — Observe clinical response to carbohydrate loading; improvement supports a glycogenolysis defect.

Explain why a patient with liver cirrhosis may develop fasting hypoglycaemia despite normal insulin levels — Damaged hepatocytes cannot perform glycogenolysis or gluconeogenesis, leading to low glucose.
ai.title: Glycogen Metabolism
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Glycogen stores glucose for rapid energy needs. Enzymes add and remove glucose units under hormonal control. Disorders alter blood sugar, cause muscle pain, or lead to life‑threatening crises.

b: Liver glycogen maintains blood glucose between meals.
Muscle glycogen fuels contraction; it does not directly raise blood glucose.
sections.p: Glycogen is a branched polymer of glucose stored mainly in liver and skeletal muscle. It provides a quick source of glucose during fasting, exercise, or stress.

b: Glycogen synthase active when dephosphorylated (insulin high).
Glycogen phosphorylase active when phosphorylated (glucagon/epinephrine high).
sections.p: Glycogen synthesis (glycogenesis) adds glucose‑1‑phosphate to a growing chain via glycogen synthase; branching enzyme creates α‑1,6 links. Glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) removes glucose‑1‑phosphate by glycogen phosphorylase; debranching enzyme handles branch points.

b: Insulin → phosphatase → dephosphorylates synthase (on) and phosphorylase (off).
Glucagon/epinephrine → cAMP → PKA → phosphorylates synthase (off) and phosphorylase (on).
sections.p: Hormones and allosteric effectors coordinate synthesis and breakdown. Insulin promotes synthesis; glucagon, epinephrine, and low ATP promote breakdown. Calcium released during muscle contraction also activates phosphorylase.

b: GSD I (von Gierke): glucose‑6‑phosphatase deficiency → severe fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis, hepatomegaly.
GSD V (McArdle): muscle phosphorylase deficiency → exercise intolerance, second‑wind phenomenon.
Hepatitis B or malaria‑induced liver injury → impaired glycogenolysis → fasting hypoglycaemia.
sections.p: Inherited enzyme defects (glycogen storage diseases, GSD) or acquired conditions (liver failure, severe infection) disrupt storage or release, producing hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, or myopathy.

t.b: Is the patient hypoglycaemic? < 70 mg/dL indicates impaired glycogenolysis or excess insulin.
Elevated (> 2 mmol/L) suggests GSD I or severe hypoxia; normal lactate makes GSD I less likely.
Raised (> 200 IU/L) after exercise points to muscle GSD (e.g., GSD V).

b: In a child with fasting seizures, consider GSD I; give frequent carbohydrate feeds.
A young adult with early fatigue on exertion may have GSD V; advise graded exercise and avoid high‑intensity bursts.
Patients with severe malaria or hepatitis may develop transient hypoglycaemia; monitor glucose closely.
sections.p: Understanding glycogen metabolism guides management of hypoglycaemia, exercise‑related muscle pain, and liver disease in low‑resource settings where advanced testing is scarce.

t.b: If meter unavailable, use urine dipstick for glucose (may miss early hypoglycaemia).
Shows hepatomegaly and bright echogenicity in GSD I; absence does not exclude disease.

b: Distinguish liver vs muscle glycogen disorders by blood glucose and CK.
Remember the ‘second‑wind’ phenomenon in McArdle disease.
In low‑resource settings, treat hypoglycaemia empirically with oral glucose before confirmatory tests.
sections.p: Focus on pattern recognition, hormonal regulation, and bedside management of hypoglycaemia.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypoglycaemia with seizures or loss of consciousness
Rhabdomyolysis causing dark urine and renal impairment
